# Results — Study 420 (Awesome Oscillator) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Bill Williams' Awesome
Oscillator (AO = SMA₅(HL2) − SMA₃₄(HL2)) turned into a long/flat timing rule: hold SPY
when AO > 0, sit in T-bills (flat 4% proxy) when AO ≤ 0, re-checked daily, entered one day
later (one execution lag). Raced against buy-and-hold and an **identical** MACD(12/26)
long/flat rule (the "does AO beat MACD?" benchmark), plus a matched-exposure random-timing
control. All Sharpe races are **excess-of-cash vs excess-of-cash**. One-way cost = 2 bps ×
NAV, charged on each switch; long-only (no borrow). SPY daily total-return OHLC
(`auto_adjust=True`), 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 (n = 8,400 days; the in-progress bar after
2026-06-12 is dropped). As-of **2026-06-13**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 | 8,400 | `9135af26d14a` |

In-market fraction: AO 66.7%, MACD 68.9%. Switches: AO 335, MACD 269 over 33 years
(~10 / ~8 round trips per year). Cash leg credited at 4%/yr flat (FRED unavailable; a
realistic conservative proxy).

## The fair race — excess-of-cash Sharpe

A long/flat rule parks in cash a third of the time, so the only honest comparison is
excess-of-cash to excess-of-cash. The random-timing control matches the AO's in-market
fraction on random days, isolating *timing skill* from mere *exposure reduction*.

| Arm | Excess CAGR | Excess Sharpe | Vol | Max drawdown (excess) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Buy-and-hold** | **+6.47%** | **+0.337** | 18.6% | −64.0% |
| AO timing | +2.12% | +0.185 | 11.4% | −39.0% |
| MACD timing | +2.85% | +0.250 | 11.3% | −43.8% |
| Random timing (null) | +3.28% | +0.211 | 15.3% | −52.4% |

*(Gross, price+dividend Sharpe — not the fair race: BH +0.553, AO +0.537, MACD +0.604.
Even on raw Sharpe the AO trails MACD and ties buy-and-hold; the cash-drag adjustment only
widens the gap.)*

## The decisive difference tests (HAC, excess returns)

| Hypothesis | Statistic | HAC *t* | Verdict |
|---|---|--:|---|
| **H1 — AO beats the index** | mean(AO − BH) excess | **−1.91** | fails (wrong sign, far from +2) |
| H2 — MACD beats the index | mean(MACD − BH) excess | −1.55 | fails |
| **H2′ — AO beats MACD** | mean(AO − MACD) excess | **−0.88** | fails (AO is *behind* MACD) |
| H3 — timing beats exposure | mean(AO − random) excess | −0.49 | fails |

- **AO vs buy-and-hold:** HAC *t* = −1.91 — the AO's excess Sharpe (+0.185) is *below*
  buy-and-hold (+0.337), and the difference points the wrong way. No real timing edge.
- **AO vs MACD:** HAC *t* = −0.88 — MACD's excess Sharpe (+0.250) is *higher* than the AO's.
  The headline "AO beats MACD" claim is false on this tape; the midpoint input buys nothing.
- **AO vs random:** HAC *t* = −0.49 — a coin out of the market as often as the AO does no
  worse. The AO's lower drawdown is exposure reduction, not skill.

## Permutation placebo (rotation, AO vs BH, gross)

Circularly rotating the AO signal to a random alignment 2,000 times (preserving its
autocorrelation and in-market fraction, breaking its alignment to returns):

| Observed AO−BH excess edge | Rotation placebo *p* |
|--:|--:|
| **−1.58 bps/day** | **0.918** |

About 92% of random rotations of the AO signal beat the real AO edge — the real alignment
is an unlucky draw from the noise distribution, not a structural signal.

## Cost sensitivity (AO excess Sharpe)

The rule is low-turnover, so costs are not what kills it — it never leads:

| One-way cost | AO excess Sharpe |
|---|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.203 |
| 1 bps | +0.194 |
| 2 bps | +0.185 |
| 5 bps | +0.158 |
| 10 bps | +0.114 |

Even gross (0 bps) the AO's excess Sharpe (+0.203) is below buy-and-hold (+0.337). The gap
is structural, not a cost artefact.

## Sub-period breakdown (excess Sharpe)

| Period | AO | MACD | Buy-and-hold |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Pre-2000 (1993–1999) | +0.26 | +0.56 | +0.99 |
| 2000s (2000–2009) | −0.08 | −0.18 | −0.22 |
| 2010s (2010–2019) | +0.13 | +0.17 | +0.58 |
| 2020s (2020–2026) | +0.58 | +0.71 | +0.50 |

The AO is least-bad in the 2000s "lost decade" and 2020s (the part-time-cash dividend),
and worst in the bull runs it sat out. It is **never the winner** of any window, and MACD
matches or beats it in every single one.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof — never market evidence)

A deterministic two-regime tape (seed=123): the planted-edge knob `edge` controls a bear
regime the trend rule can step out of.

| Tape | AO excess Sharpe | BH excess Sharpe | *t* (AO − BH) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Null (single regime, edge=0) | +0.719 | +0.963 | **−4.23** |
| Planted bears (edge=1.5) | −0.120 | −0.401 | **+2.57** |

On the null tape the AO rule correctly *loses* to buy-and-hold (a trend filter cannot beat
a single-regime drift). On the planted-bear tape it banks a real edge (*t* = +2.57,
drawdown cut from −100% to −79%). **The harness can detect a genuine timing edge** — its
failure to find one on SPY is informative, not a power problem.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The AO long/flat rule's excess Sharpe (+0.185) is *below* buy-and-hold
  (+0.337); the difference HAC *t* = −1.91 has the wrong sign and is far from the +2 bar. A
  rotation permutation places the observed edge at *p* = 0.92. There is no certifiable timing
  signal in the AO on SPY.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The AO loses the race even gross, and worse net. Its only real
  effect is exposure reduction: a random coin out of the market as often (+0.211) sits right
  beside it (+0.185), and the lower drawdown (−39% vs −64%) is paid for with lower return
  (+2.1% vs +6.5% excess CAGR). Nothing to scale.
- **Beats MACD? — BUSTED.** MACD's excess Sharpe (+0.250) is *higher* than the AO's (+0.185);
  the AO−MACD difference *t* = −0.88. The "leading indicator beats the lagging MACD" marketing
  is simply false here — the midpoint input carries no edge over the close-based MACD, and if
  anything the MACD is marginally better.
